meta.trial_name: VITAL (Vitamin D and Omega-3 Trial), omega-3 comparison
meta.drug: marine omega-3 fatty acids ONLY (omega-3 arm of the 2x2 factorial VITAL trial): Omacor (Lovaza in the U.S.) fish oil 1 g/day, 840 mg EPA+DHA (460-465 mg EPA + 375-380 mg DHA) vs omega-3 placebo; the vitamin D3 2000 IU/day factor is a separate comparison and is not this case
meta.sponsor: Brigham and Women's Hospital (academic; NIH-funded: NCI, NHLBI, ODS, NINDS, NCCIH; study agents donated by Pronova BioPharma/BASF (Omacor) and Pharmavite (vitamin D))
meta.mechanism: Omega-3 arm of VITAL: low-dose (1 g/day) marine omega-3 fatty acids (EPA + DHA) as a dietary-supplement-type primary prevention strategy. No single molecular target; the trial authors list anti-thrombotic, hypotriglyceridemic, blood-pressure-lowering, anti-inflammatory, anti-arrhythmic and endothelial mechanisms (S1). At 1 g/day the triglyceride-lowering effect is small (about 5.9 mg/dL per 1 g/day in a dose-response analysis of 58 placebo-controlled trials, S7/S11). target_symbol LPL is used only as the human-genetic proxy for the triglyceride-lowering pathway (Ference 2019 LPL Mendelian randomization, S14), as in the STRENGTH case; it is not a confirmed drug target. The vitamin D3 factor of VITAL is not part of this case.
meta.modality: oral fish-oil capsule (omega-3-acid ethyl esters, Omacor/Lovaza), one 1-g capsule daily
meta.indication: primary prevention of major cardiovascular events (MI, stroke, CV death) in a general, usual-risk U.S. population: men >=50 and women >=55 years without prior cardiovascular disease or cancer (20% African American)

n_randomized.unit: patients (whole factorial trial; omega-3 12,933 vs omega-3 placebo 12,938)
n_randomized.quote: A total of 25,871 participants, including 5106 black participants, underwent randomization.
n_randomized.note: Arm sizes from Table 2 header: n-3 (N = 12,933), Placebo (N = 12,938); registry S3 denominators 12933 / 12938.

median_followup.quote: Study medication ceased as planned on December 31, 2017, yielding a median intervention period of 5.3 years (range 3.8-6.1 years).
median_followup.note: Abstract: 'During a median follow-up of 5.3 years'.

primary_endpoint.value: Major cardiovascular events: composite of myocardial infarction, stroke, or death from cardiovascular causes (co-primary with invasive cancer of any type)
primary_endpoint.quote: Primary end points were major cardiovascular events (a composite of myocardial infarction, stroke, or death from cardiovascular causes) and invasive cancer of any type.
primary_endpoint.note: This case uses only the cardiovascular primary end point of the omega-3 vs placebo comparison. Secondary: expanded composite (+ coronary revascularization), MI, stroke, CV death.

inclusion_key_criteria.value: Men aged >=50 or women aged >=55; no history of cancer (except non-melanoma skin cancer), MI, stroke, TIA, angina, CABG or PCI; no fish or soy allergy; not taking fish-oil supplements (or willing to stop)
inclusion_key_criteria.quote: be men aged 50 or older or women aged 55 or older;
inclusion_key_criteria.note: Registry S3 also: 'have no history of cancer (except non-melanoma skin cancer), heart attack, stroke, transient ischemic attack, angina pectoris, coronary-artery bypass grafting, or percutaneous coronary intervention;' and 'not be taking fish oil supplements, or, if taking, willing to forego their use during the trial'. Not selected on vascular risk factors (S1 Introduction).

planned_events.note: NOT FOUND: the design paper (S4) gives power for an observed rate ratio, not a planned number of events. Observed in the omega-3 comparison: 805 major CV events (386 + 419).

assumed_rrr.quote: Assuming that only one agent is effective, there will be 86% power to detect an observed rate ratio (RR) of 0.85 for the primary cancer endpoint of total cancer incidence (Table 1) and 89% power to detect an observed RR of 0.80 for the primary cardiovascular endpoint
assumed_rrr.note: Assumed 80% compliance, so 'true' RR 0.75. Design Table 2 (major CVD): power 34.6% for an observed RR of 0.90, 66.1% for 0.85, 89.4% for 0.80 (values read from the table). Companion vitamin D paper S5: 'VITAL was designed to have >85% power to detect observed hazard ratios (HR) of 0.85 and 0.80 for the primary cancer and cardiovascular endpoints, respectively.' Design assumed 20,000 participants; 25,871 were enrolled.

power.quote: 89% power to detect an observed RR of 0.80 for the primary cardiovascular endpoint
power.note: Power computed for 20,000 participants over 5 years; S5 says '>85% power'. Only ~35% power for an observed RR of 0.90 (design Table 2).

alpha.quote: Power was computed for a two-sided test using a logrank analysis [107] with a significance level of 0.05.
alpha.note: S1: 'There was no control for multiple hypothesis testing, with no formal adjustment to the p-values or confidence intervals.' Two co-primary end points and two factors were each tested at 0.05.

stopped_early.quote: Study medication ceased as planned on December 31, 2017, yielding a median intervention period of 5.3 years (range 3.8-6.1 years).
stopped_early.note: Completed as planned; not stopped early.

baseline.biomarker: omega-3 index (plasma EPA+DHA as % of total fatty acids)
baseline.quote: Among the 15,535 participants with analyzable baseline blood samples (60%), the mean plasma omega-3 index was 2.67% (SD, 0.9%) in both groups.
In VITAL lipid parameters were calculated in the sample of size 15,965
baseline.note: Value read from the 'VITAL' column of Table 1 of the VITAL200 substudy paper (whole-trial blood sample, n=15,965): LDLC 124 (102-148) mg/dL = 3.2 mmol/L (derived). Not reported in the main NEJM paper (S1).

baseline.quote: In VITAL lipid parameters were calculated in the sample of size 15,965
baseline.note: Trig 111 (83-155) mg/dL = 1.25 mmol/L (derived). Normal-range triglycerides: VITAL did not select for hypertriglyceridemia.

baseline.quote: In VITAL lipid parameters were calculated in the sample of size 15,965
baseline.note: Total cholesterol 204 (179-232) mg/dL in the same column.
NOT FOUND: baseline apoB not reported in S1 or S17.
NOT FOUND as a reported median (TC 204 and HDL-C 52 medians are given; a difference of medians is not the median non-HDL-C).

biomarker_effects.biomarker: omega-3 index (plasma EPA+DHA % of total fatty acids)
biomarker_effects.method: plasma omega-3 index, LC-MS/MS (Quest Diagnostics), n=1,583 with baseline and 1-year samples
biomarker_effects.quote: Among the 1,583 participants who also provided an analyzable one-year blood sample, the mean omega-3 index rose to 4.13% (54.7% increase) in the active group and changed <2% in the placebo group.
biomarker_effects.note: Adherence / exposure biomarker, not a causal risk factor in the calculator. change_abs 1.46 percentage points is DERIVED (4.13 - 2.67, within the active arm). Within-arm change; placebo changed <2%. VITAL200 substudy (S17, RBC assay): EPA +111.8% and omega-3 index +50.7% median in the n-3 arm vs about -1% in placebo at 1 year.

NOT FOUND: no placebo-adjusted triglyceride (or LDL-C, apoB, non-HDL-C) change for the VITAL omega-3 arm was found in the NEJM paper (S1), the VITAL200 substudy (S17, which reports only associations with lipid changes) or other searched VITAL papers. The NEJM Supplementary Appendix could not be accessed (HTTP 403).

biomarker_effects.timepoint: dose-response across placebo-controlled trials (not VITAL data)
biomarker_effects.method: external evidence: dose-response meta-analysis of 58 placebo-controlled trials (Mozaffarian & Wu 2011, S11), as cited by Hu, Hu & Manson 2019 (S7)
biomarker_effects.quote: A dose–response analysis based on 58 placebo‐controlled trials estimated that each 1 g/d increase of marine omega‐3 reduced triglyceride levels by 5.9 mg/dL and such linear association did not plateau even at 7 g/d.
biomarker_effects.note: Expected (not observed) effect of the VITAL dose (840 mg EPA+DHA, about 1 g/day), available before readout (S11, 2011). change_pct -5.3 is DERIVED as -5.9 / 111 mg/dL (VITAL baseline median, S17). In mmol/L: -0.067 (DERIVED, /88.57). Secondary citation: the original analysis (S11) was not read in full. 'phase2' here labels pre-readout external evidence, not a VITAL phase 2 study (none exists).

biomarker_effects.timepoint: dose-response across placebo-controlled trials (not VITAL data)
biomarker_effects.method: external evidence; DERIVED unit conversion of the row above
biomarker_effects.quote: each 1 g/d increase of marine omega‐3 reduced triglyceride levels by 5.9 mg/dL
biomarker_effects.note: Same value as above in mmol/L (5.9 / 88.57 = 0.067).

biomarker_effects.method: hsCRP, IL-6, TNFR2 in 1,561 VITAL participants
biomarker_effects.quote: Neither supplement reduced biomarkers at 1 year.
biomarker_effects.note: No significant reduction of hsCRP, IL-6 or TNFR2 with n-3 FA at 1 year; overall percent change for the n-3 arm not given in the abstract. In low fish eaters hsCRP -10.5% (-20.4% to 0.8%). Abstract only.

hr.unit: hazard ratio (primary end point: major cardiovascular events, omega-3 vs placebo)
hr.quote: During a median follow-up of 5.3 years, a major cardiovascular event occurred in 386 participants in the n-3 group and in 419 in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.92; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.80 to 1.06; P=0.24).
hr.note: Registry S3 identical: HR 0.92 (0.80-1.06), p=0.24 (Cox). Secondary: total MI HR 0.72 (0.59-0.90; 145 vs 200), total stroke 1.04 (0.83-1.31), CV death 0.96 (0.76-1.21), expanded composite 0.93 (0.82-1.04), PCI 0.78 (0.63-0.95), fatal MI 0.50 (0.26-0.97), total CHD 0.83 (0.71-0.97) (S1 Table 2; no multiplicity adjustment). Excluding first 2 years: MACE HR 0.89 (0.76-1.05).

p.quote: hazard ratio, 0.92; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.80 to 1.06; P=0.24

events_treatment.quote: a major cardiovascular event occurred in 386 participants in the n-3 group

events_control.quote: and in 419 in the placebo group

safety_signals.value: No excess bleeding, gastrointestinal symptoms or other serious adverse events with omega-3
safety_signals.quote: No excess risks of bleeding or other serious adverse events were observed.
safety_signals.note: Results: 'The intervention was not associated with significant differences in gastrointestinal symptoms, major bleeding episodes, or other serious side effects, compared to placebo'.

safety_signals.value: Cancer: no effect overall (HR 1.03, 0.93-1.13); excluding the first 2 years HR 1.13 (1.00-1.28), nonsignificant, no increase in cancer death
safety_signals.quote: In analyses excluding the first two years of follow-up, the HRs were 1.13 (1.00-1.28) for cancer incidence and 0.93([0.0.73-1.19) for cancer mortality in the n-3 group (Table 2).
safety_signals.note: Exploratory; the authors call it a nonsignificant increase in cancer incidence. Quote reproduces a typo in the author manuscript.
Read from Table 2 (row 'Hemorrhagic stroke | 25 | 19 | 1.32 | 0.72-2.39'); not prespecified. Total stroke HR 1.04 (0.83-1.31).

safety_signals.value: Atrial fibrillation (VITAL Rhythm ancillary study): 469 vs 431, HR 1.09 (0.96-1.24), not significant
safety_signals.quote: For the EPA-DHA vs placebo comparison, incident AF events occurred in 469 (3.7%) vs 431 (3.4%) participants, respectively (hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.96-1.24; P = .19).

genetics.finding: No single molecular target for fish oil; no target-specific human genetics. A post-readout two-sample Mendelian randomization study (5 SNPs for circulating omega-3) found genetically lower circulating omega-3 associated with higher MI risk, but the MR-Egger estimate was null with a wide CI.
genetics.effect: IVW OR 1.224 (1.045-1.433) for MI per genetically lower omega-3; MR-Egger OR 0.950 (0.513-1.760)
genetics.quote: The genetically predicted lower circulating omega-3 increased the risk of myocardial infarction showed by the results of IVW [odds ratio (OR) = 1.224, 95% CI = 1.045-1.433, P = 0.012]
genetics.note: Abstract only. Weak evidence (5 instruments, small exposure GWAS of 13,544). Not available before readout.

genetics.finding: Rare APOC3 loss-of-function mutations lower triglycerides by 39% and are associated with 40% lower CHD risk, supporting a causal role of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins
genetics.quote: The risk of coronary heart disease among 498 carriers of any rare APOC3 mutation was 40% lower than the risk among 110,472 noncarriers (odds ratio, 0.60; 95% confidence interval, 0.47 to 0.75; P=4×10(-6)).
genetics.note: PRE-readout. Abstract read (Europe PMC). Lifelong large TG reduction; 1 g/day fish oil lowers TG only a few mg/dL.

genetics.finding: Mendelian randomization: TG-lowering LPL variants protect only in proportion to the apoB lowering; TG has no association with CHD after adjusting for apoB
genetics.effect: OR 0.771 (0.741-0.802) per 10 mg/dL lower apoB via LPL score; TG adjusted for apoB OR 1.014 (0.965-1.065)
genetics.quote: Triglyceride-lowering LPL variants and LDL-C-lowering LDLR variants were associated with similar lower risk of CHD per unit difference in ApoB. Therefore, the clinical benefit of lowering triglyceride and LDL-C levels may be proportional to the absolute change in ApoB.
genetics.note: POST-readout (JAMA 2019;321(4), Jan 2019; Europe PMC lists 2019-01). Abstract read. With a TG change of only ~6 mg/dL expected at 1 g/day, the apoB change (not measured in VITAL) would be negligible, predicting almost no lipid-mediated benefit.

consensus_explanation.summary: VITAL's omega-3 comparison was a true neutral result for its primary end point: 1 g/day of fish oil (840 mg EPA+DHA) gave a major cardiovascular event HR of 0.92 (0.80-1.06), in a usual-risk primary-prevention population with only 805 events, and the trial had been powered (89%) for an observed rate ratio of 0.80, with only about 35% power for a 10% reduction. Experts read the observed effect as consistent with the small benefit seen in meta-analyses of moderate-dose omega-3 (about 3% for total CVD and major vascular events; Hu, Hu & Manson 2019 including VITAL), with a dose-response relationship suggesting that benefit needs higher doses. At 1 g/day the triglyceride-lowering effect is only about 6 mg/dL, and neither triglyceride nor apoB changes were reported in VITAL; inflammation markers did not fall at 1 year. The composite end point mixed outcomes that responded (total MI HR 0.72, fatal MI 0.50, PCI 0.78) with outcomes that did not (stroke HR 1.04, CV death 0.96), so stroke and CV death diluted the coronary signal. The trialists and meta-analysts treat the MI reduction and the larger benefit in low fish eaters and African Americans as hypothesis-generating, because there was no multiplicity adjustment. ASCEND (1 g/day, diabetes, null) and earlier meta-analyses had already pointed to a weak effect at this dose before the readout.
consensus_explanation.review_note: Primary effect_too_small: the expected benefit of 1 g/day omega-3 (a few percent) was far below the RR 0.80 the trial was powered for. Secondary design_or_endpoint: stroke and CV death, which omega-3 did not reduce, diluted the composite (MI alone HR 0.72). Secondary population: low-risk primary prevention with low event rates, and benefit concentrated in low fish eaters (subgroup). The NEJM editorial (S6) could not be read, so it does not inform this summary.

pre_readout.note: Facts with a public source dated before readout_date (2018-11-10).
available_before_readout: Registry record with both primary end points and eligibility (S3, first posted 2010-07-26)
Design and power: 89% power for an observed RR of 0.80 on major CVD, ~35% for RR 0.90, two-sided alpha 0.05, 1 g/day Omacor (S4, 2011-10-02)
Dose-response of TG lowering ~5.9 mg/dL per 1 g/day omega-3 (Mozaffarian & Wu, S11, 2011-11-01)
APOC3 loss-of-function genetics: lower TG and 40% lower CHD (S15, 2014-06-18)
Aung 2018 meta-analysis of 10 trials: no significant effect of omega-3 on major vascular events, RR 0.97 (S9, 2018-03-01)
ASCEND: 1 g/day omega-3 in diabetes, serious vascular events rate ratio 0.97 (0.87-1.08) (S10, 2018-08-26)
only_after_readout: VITAL omega-3 outcome HR 0.92 (0.80-1.06), events 386 vs 419, MI HR 0.72, omega-3 index +54.7% (S1, 2018-11-10, same day as readout)
Inflammation markers not reduced at 1 year (S12, 2019-11-07)
Updated meta-analysis including VITAL with dose-response (S7, 2019-09-30; S8, 2020-09-17)
LPL Mendelian randomization: TG benefit proportional to apoB (S14, 2019-01)
VITAL baseline lipids (S17, 2020-10-27); AF ancillary result (S13, 2021-03-01); omega-3 MR (S16, 2024-03-14)

sources.note: Participant-facing findings page of the trial team, read live. Earliest Wayback capture 2018-11-12 (https://web.archive.org/web/20181112133612/https://www.vitalstudy.org/findings.html); exact posting date unknown, so not used as the topline announcement. Omega-3: 'an 8% reduction that was not significant'; low fish intake subgroup 'a 19% reduction in major cardiovascular events, including a 40% reduction in heart attack'.

open_questions: No placebo-adjusted triglyceride, LDL-C, apoB or non-HDL-C change for the VITAL omega-3 arm was found; the calculator input uses an external dose-response estimate (5.9 mg/dL TG per 1 g/day, S7 citing S11), which is not VITAL data. The NEJM Supplementary Appendix (nejm.org, HTTP 403) was not read.
Planned number of events not stated; the design paper (S4) sized the trial for 20,000 participants and an observed RR of 0.80 (89% power); 25,871 were enrolled.
No multiplicity control (S1): the MI reduction (HR 0.72) and the subgroup benefits (low fish intake, African Americans) are hypothesis-generating; the press release (S2) headlines the MI result.
The NEJM editorial (S6, Keaney & Rosen) could not be read.
The BWH press release has no Wayback capture from 2018-11-10; the earliest is 2019-05-08. The live URL now redirects to an unrelated news home page.

Expert explanations differ on emphasis: dose too low (S7, S8) versus a genuinely small effect of moderate-dose EPA+DHA on composite end points (S9, S10). No source attributes the null result to poor adherence (81.6% vs 81.5% adherence, outside fish-oil use <3.5%).
